doc.title: Phil Schaap interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

chapter: Becoming an audio man and DJ
title: Meeting Jamie Katz at Columbia
summary: Jamie Katz blindfold tests Phil in the dorm; Phil names McCoy Tyner and Dick Katz.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man

blocks.x: Right. Well you got into the radio through Columbia University.

Absolutely. And through my sound career. But when I got to Columbia most of the people in Furnald, the dormitory I lived in, they didn’t really know what I was playing but they knew it wasn’t what they were used to listening to and they vaguely understood it was jazz and everybody kept saying that I should go see Jamie Katz, who lived, well I was on 1006 Fernald and he lived in, like it was interconnected, I think it was 732, 33, 34. They reconfigured the doors but not the rooms in that building so it’s all moved now anyway. But he was down on the seventh floor. And one night I went down there and I knocked on his door and he blindfold tested me. So the first thing he played — actually he almost could have got me but I knew it, I knew it was McCoy. So I says, “That’s McCoy Tyner.” He said, “Pretty good.” He says, “I’m going to give you a hard one now.” And then he played — I even know the record he was playing, I told him I knew the record. I didn’t see it, I mean he was blindfold testing me, but it was Count Basie with Bennie Moten’s band. I mean it was sort of like “The Briar Patch Story.” So I said, “Well that’s Count Basie playing a little combination Fats Waller and four hands in his early records with Benny Moten’s Kansas City Orchestra, of ‘Jones Law Blues’ and ‘Small Black’” and that was — so then he says, “now I’m going to play you another record” and he said, “and I want you to tell me who the piano player is on it. I know you’ll recognized © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

the others because you seem to know the stuff.” So he puts on “Further Definitions” Benny Carter, Impulse Records and so I said, “The piano player, that’s Dick Katz.” And he goes, “How do you know that.” I said well “Richard Aaron Katz, March 13, 1924, Baltimore Maryland, played a lot with Tony Scott and was well known for association with Orrin Keepnews and Milestone Records and I don’t know whether he had started his association with Helen Merrill at that time but if he had I would have known about it and I would have said something. And he’s on Benny Carter’s ‘Further Definitions’ records and also played with Buck Clayton at the Newport Jazz Festival,” which I should have said actually he played with the J.J. Johnson band at the Newport Jazz Festival. They happened to make a record with Buck Clayton. But that’s how I knew him from that period. And then I said, “Of course he’s Roy Eldridge’s piano player.” And I stopped with that. And he said, “Oh yeah, that’s my father.”
Oh it was Dick Katz’s son, oh my.
Okay well then you were winning some points. But you didn’t know it at the time.
No. Katz is a very common last name, K-A-T-Z is a common last name in New York City. I wasn’t thinking what Jamie’s last name was anyway, I was thinking I’ve got to get these questions right.
So I said who Dick Katz was and there I was.
